rationale: Across multiple cohorts, FBXO11-associated neurodevelopmental disorder (IDDFBA, OMIM #618089) is driven primarily by loss-of-function variants (nonsense, frameshift, splice site, and whole/partial gene deletions) and missense variants that result in loss of function via protein destabilization, cytoplasmic mislocalization, or reduced expression. Functional assays in HEK293/HeLa cells demonstrate that missense variants localized to key domains (such as the F-box and Zn-finger UBR domains) impair normal localization and stability, confirming haploinsufficiency as the shared primary pathogenic mechanism across variant classes. Clinical series (Gregor et al. 2018, Jansen et al. 2019, Gregor et al. 2022, Goel et al. 2026) show that the core phenotype—characterized by developmental delay/intellectual disability, behavioral disturbances, hypotonia, and subtle facial features (e.g., thin upper lip with broad prominent philtrum)—is shared across variant types without established genotype-phenotype divergence.

evidence.text: In a cohort of 20 individuals with de novo FBXO11 alterations, the mutational spectrum comprises two large deletions, ten likely gene-disrupting variants, and eight missense variants distributed across the gene (including CASH and Zinc-finger UBR domains). Structural modeling indicated protein destabilization, and the absence of apparent genotype-phenotype correlations supported haploinsufficiency as the primary mechanism.

source.title: De novo variants in the F-box protein FBXO11 in 20 individuals with a variable neurodevelopmental disorder
source.journal: The American Journal of Human Genetics
source.quote: The identified de novo aberrations comprise two large deletions, ten likely gene disrupting variants, and eight missense variants distributed throughout FBXO11. Structural modeling for missense variants located in the CASH or the Zinc-finger UBR domains suggests destabilization of the protein. This, in combination with the observed spectrum and localization of identified variants and the lack of apparent genotype-phenotype correlations, is compatible with loss of function or haploinsufficiency as an underlying mechanism.

evidence.text: Assessment of 24 individuals identified de novo variants including 2 partial deletions, 8 nonsense/frameshift variants, 1 canonical splice site variant, 2 in-frame deletions, and 11 missense variants. All 24 patients presented with borderline to severe intellectual disability, high rates of behavioral problems, hypotonia, joint hyperlaxity, and characteristic upper lip dysmorphisms without distinct phenotype divergence between truncating and missense variants.

source.title: De novo variants in FBXO11 cause a syndromic form of intellectual disability with behavioral problems and dysmorphisms
source.quote: Twenty-two variants were identified by next-generation sequencing, comprising 2 in-frame deletions, 11 missense variants, 1 canonical splice site variant, and 8 nonsense or frameshift variants leading to a truncated protein or degraded transcript. The remaining two variants were identified by array-comparative genomic hybridization and consisted of a partial deletion of FBXO11. All individuals had borderline to severe ID and behavioral problems (autism spectrum disorder, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, anxiety, aggression) were observed in most of them.

evidence.text: Functional analysis of 17 missense variants across FBXO11 in 23 additional individuals demonstrated that variants in the N-terminal F-box domain and NLS cause exclusion from the nucleus, cytoplasmic aggregation, and reduced protein levels, whereas variants in the C-terminal Zn-finger UBR domain cause cytoplasmic accumulation. Both mechanisms disrupt normal nuclear SCF complex function, affirming haploinsufficiency as the shared mechanism without distinct genotype-phenotype divergence.

source.title: De novo missense variants in FBXO11 alter its protein expression and subcellular localization
source.quote: Together with the mutational data, our functional results suggest that most missense variants likely lead to a loss of the original FBXO11 function and thereby highlight haploinsufficiency as the most likely disease mechanism for FBXO11-associated NDDs.

evidence.text: A study of 21 newly reported individuals with missense (8), nonsense (5), and multi-exon deletions identified mild ID (86%), facial dysmorphism (67%), hypotonia (62%), and behavioral dysregulation (62%), reiterating that haploinsufficiency is the unifying pathogenic mechanism.

source.title: Defining FBXO11-Related Neurodevelopmental Disorder: Clinical, Molecular and Facial Assessment of 21 Patients
source.quote: Variants included missense, truncating, and multi-exon deletions, supporting haploinsufficiency as the principal pathogenic mechanism.

evidence.text: Identification of an autosomal dominantly inherited heterozygous frameshift variant (c.2401_2405dup; p.Gly803Leufs*6) transmitted from a mother to two affected daughters demonstrates that while most cases arise de novo, transmitted truncating variants also cause IDDFBA.

new_directions.question_text: Does subcellular partitioning difference between N-terminal/F-box variants (nuclear exclusion and degradation) and C-terminal UBR variants (cytoplasmic accumulation) translate into subtle differences in metabolic or growth phenotypes such as obesity?
new_directions.rationale: Gregor et al. (2022) identified distinct molecular cellular behaviors between domains and suggested possible correlations with obesity, warranting systematic metabolic evaluation across large cohorts.

new_directions.question_text: Can computational facial phenotyping (e.g., GestaltMatcher) reliably discriminate FBXO11-related disorder from clinically overlapping neurodevelopmental disorders sharing hypotonia and behavioral dysregulation?
new_directions.rationale: Because facial dysmorphism is subtle and cognitive phenotypes overlap broadly with other neurodevelopmental syndromes, objective quantitative gestalt scoring may facilitate pre-test syndromic identification.
